data.content_ref: inline:The target's justification is internally self-defeating. The claim says we prefer better-corroborated theories because doing so 'maximizes the potential for learning from error (falsification).' But a theory that has withstood more severe tests is, by the target's own non-inductive framework, one for which we have NO basis to expect future falsification. If corroboration provides no inductive purchase on the future (as the claim insists), then a better-corroborated theory offers no greater—and arguably lesser—potential for future learning-by-falsification, since it has already survived the tests most likely to expose its errors. The stated rationale thus undercuts itself: maximizing 'potential for learning from error' would favor LESS corroborated (less tested) theories, which have more unexplored avenues for refutation. Furthermore, the mechanism is explicitly circular: it concludes, 'The reason this holds is that Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms... which is what the mechanism above establishes.' It restates the claim as its own justification rather than supplying independent support. It also asserts that when a highly corroborated theory fails, 'the loss of information is greater,' framing a COST as the BENEFIT ('maximizing learning') without explaining the inversion.
